extracted.intended_audience: literary readers, writers, and prospective contributors to The Paris Review
extracted.subtask_description: Historical editorial mission and content-selection preferences of The Paris Review: emphasizes creative work (fiction and poetry), editorial stance on criticism, preference for certain kinds of writers, and use of long-form author interviews. Useful for understanding what the magazine values when producing and selecting material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize creative work (fiction and poetry)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Paris Review hopes to emphasize creative work—fiction and poetry—not to the exclusion of criticism, but with the aim in mind of merely removing criticism from the dominating place it holds in most literary magazines and putting it pretty much where it belongs, i.e., somewhere near the back of the book."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial mission: foreground original creative work over criticism; criticism is permitted but should not dominate the magazine's pages and should be de-emphasized in placement and prominence.

rubrics_metrics.name: De-emphasize dominating criticism / place criticism toward the back
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism should be "removed from the dominating place it holds in most literary magazines and put... somewhere near the back of the book."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical production guideline: include criticism sparingly and organize the magazine so that critical pieces are less prominent (e.g., placed after primary creative content).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize "good writers and good poets" (avoid agitprop/drumbeaters)
rubrics_metrics.description: "I think The Paris Review should welcome these people into its pages: the good writers and good poets, the non-drumbeaters and non-axe-grinders. So long as they're good."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection preference emphasizes literary quality and craft over polemical or attention-seeking voices; the magazine favors serious, skillful writers rather than noisy or agenda-driven contributors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use long-form author interviews to let writers discuss craft and life
rubrics_metrics.description: The Review’s Writers at Work interview series offers authors a rare opportunity to discuss their life and art at length; they have responded with some of the most revealing self-portraits in literature. In the words of one critic, it is “one of the single most persistent acts of cultural conservation in the history of the world.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial practice: include extended, in-depth interviews with authors that focus on craft, process, and artistic life as a core component of the magazine’s contribution to literary culture and as a way to preserve authorial self-reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform emerging and significant writers / publish early important works
rubrics_metrics.description: "Decade after decade, the Review has introduced the important writers of the day." Examples cited include early publications or selections from works by Adrienne Rich, Philip Roth, V. S. Naipaul, Samuel Beckett, Jack Kerouac, Italo Calvino, Donald Barthelme, Jeffrey Eugenides, Jonathan Franzen, and others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial outcome/criterion: the magazine seeks and publishes work that may be formative or seminal in an author's career — early or important pieces that contribute to the literary canon; editorial acquisitions often include notable early stories, novel excerpts, and other milestone works.
